clue.text: Book distressing a dutiful mourner

indicators.note: distressing in the sense of roughing up or damaging, so these letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A sad book that upsets a conscientious mourner at a funeral.
explanation.walkthrough: 'distressing' looks like an adjective for the book, but it is the anagram signal on A DUTIFUL MOURNER.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the title of the last novel Charles Dickens completed, so it is a book.

clue.text: Con man left in second part of watch

indicators.note: in says the letter for left goes inside the watch part

parts.note: the winder is the crown you turn to wind a watch

explanation.surface: A conman leaves something inside the second part of a wristwatch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second part of watch' reads as one phrase, but 'second' gives S on its own and 'part of watch' is the winder.
explanation.definitionFit: A swindler cheats people out of money, which is exactly what a con man does.

clue.text: Grim black hole

parts.note: B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
a hole in a pipe or boat is a leak

explanation.surface: A black hole is a grim, inescapable place.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonyms: a grim outlook or prospect is a bleak one, offering no hope.

clue.text: Special troops fooled fall guy finally using foul means

parts.note: OR, other ranks, is the military term for ordinary troops
to do someone is slang for cheating them, so did means fooled

indicators.note: finally takes the last letter of each of the two words before it

explanation.surface: Special forces tricked a scapegoat by underhand means.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall guy' looks like one unit (a scapegoat), but 'finally' takes the end of each word, L and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in a sordid way is acting dishonourably, by base or underhand methods.

clue.text: Notice large worker's collared parish officer

indicators.note: collared means grabbed round the neck, so the insect holds the other letters inside

parts.note: a bee is the crossword's standard worker; the 's is read as 'is'
an ad is a notice in a paper
L is the abbreviation for large, as on clothing

explanation.surface: A big notice announces that some worker has been arrested by a parish official.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collared' sounds like an arrest, but it means the worker wraps round the notice and the size.
explanation.definitionFit: A beadle was a minor official of a parish, keeping order in church, as in Mr Bumble in Oliver Twist.

clue.text: Idiot coming in without monarch's blessing

parts.note: an ass is a fool

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the monarch's letters are dropped

parts.note: entering means coming in
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the crossword monarch; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A fool arrives in the absence of the king's or queen's approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' tells you to remove ER from ASSENTERING, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Blessing a plan, as a verb, means giving it your approval, or agreeing to it.

clue.text: He evades magistrate jailing Democrat and Republican

indicators.note: jailing means locking up, so the Democrat's letter goes inside the magistrate

parts.note: the doge was the chief magistrate of Venice or Genoa
D is the abbreviation for a US Democrat
R is the abbreviation for a US Republican

explanation.surface: A man escapes justice while a judge imprisons two American politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who dodges, as a tax or draft dodger does, is a person who evades things.

clue.text: Book translates it as 'Lorca's Charm'

indicators.note: translates suggests turning words into another form, so these letters are rendered in a new order

explanation.surface: A translator renders a book under the Spanish-sounding title Lorca's Charm.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorca the Spanish poet is a red herring: 'translates' is the anagram signal on IT AS LORCAS CHARM.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Charles Dickens's 1843 festive novella about Scrooge, so it is a book.

clue.text: New column we put in close to mine's not liked

indicators.note: new means freshly made, so these letters are formed anew in another order
close to means the end of the word mine, its last letter

explanation.surface: A newspaper's new column written by us, placed near the colliery, is unpopular.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' is the anagram signal on COLUMN WE plus E, the last letter of 'mine'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unwelcome is not wanted or received gladly, so it is disliked.

clue.text: Patient, small one in bed, having a turn

indicators.note: in places the numeral inside the turned-round bed
having a turn means being turned round, so the word cot reads backwards

parts.note: a cot is a small bed
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A patient, a little one in a hospital bed, is having a funny turn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Patient' looks like a hospital patient, a noun, but it is the adjective: COT turned round is TOC, and I goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoic person endures hardship calmly without complaint, which is to say patiently.

clue.text: Nip back across a new style attic

indicators.note: across means the turned-round drink lies across, around, the other letters
back means the word dram is read backwards

parts.note: a nip of whisky is a dram
NS stands for New Style, the Gregorian calendar dating

explanation.surface: A quick drink brought back to a newly fashionable loft.
explanation.walkthrough: New Style refers to the Gregorian calendar, adopted in Britain in 1752; 'across' means the reversed drink straddles the other letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A mansard is a roof with two slopes, and also the attic room under such a roof.

clue.text: Drive trimmer that clears beds

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for drive in street names
an edger is a garden tool for trimming lawn edges

explanation.surface: A gardening tool that tidies up the flower beds.
explanation.walkthrough: The beds are not flower beds but river and sea beds.
explanation.definitionFit: A dredger is a vessel that scoops silt from the floors of rivers and harbours.

clue.text: Almost incredible English fiction

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: a tall story is an incredible one

explanation.surface: A piece of English fiction that is very nearly unbelievable.
explanation.definitionFit: A tale is a story, a piece of fiction, often an invented one.

clue.text: Exploits appearance on American screens

parts.note: an advent is an arrival or appearance

indicators.note: screens means shields or hides, so the American letters hold the other two inside

parts.note: re means on, about, as in letters

explanation.surface: A film star exploits an appearance on American screens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploits' looks like a verb but is the noun, and 'screens' is a verb here, not cinema screens.
explanation.definitionFit: Exploits are daring deeds, and adventures are exciting or risky undertakings.

clue.text: Thief initially lambasts another criminal on radio

indicators.note: initially takes the first letter of the word lambasts
on radio means heard, so the criminal's name is spelt by its sound

parts.note: an arsonist is a criminal who starts fires

explanation.surface: A thief first lays into a fellow crook in a radio broadcast.
explanation.definitionFit: Larceny is the legal term for theft, so someone who commits it is a thief.

clue.text: A woman has received note by now

indicators.note: has received means the woman takes in the note

parts.note: a lady is a woman
re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A woman has got a letter by now.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note' is a musical note, not a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Already means before now or by this time, a direct synonym of the phrase.

clue.text: Sonny hurt writer's back — or rear, say?

indicators.note: hurt means damaged, so the letters of Sonny are knocked out of order
back means the word my is read backwards

parts.note: the writer's means the setter's, my

explanation.surface: Sonny injured the writer's back, or perhaps the rear?
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' does two jobs in the surface: it reverses MY, and rear is offered as a word meaning back.
explanation.definitionFit: Rear is an example of a word with the same meaning as another, here back.

clue.text: One who ridicules It Girl in Times

parts.note: SA, sex appeal, is old slang for It

indicators.note: in places the girl's name inside the two Ts

parts.note: T is time, so two Ts are times
Iris is a girl's name

explanation.surface: An It Girl mocked in The Times newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It Girl' reads as one phrase, a glamorous socialite, but splits in two; 'It' as sex appeal is old slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A satirist mocks people or institutions through humour, irony and exaggeration.

clue.text: Short pleasant vacation entertaining a saint

indicators.note: short means cut off, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: nice means pleasant

indicators.note: entertaining means hosting, so the holiday word holds the letter a

parts.note: hols is British slang for holidays

explanation.surface: A brief pleasant holiday spent playing host to a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: HOLS is everyday British for holidays, so the vacation word is HOLS with A inside.
explanation.definitionFit: St Nicholas, the patron saint of children, is the origin of Santa Claus.

clue.text: Cops in Florida town showing lack of vigour

indicators.note: in puts the police letters inside the town

parts.note: a city is a large town
CID, the Criminal Investigation Department, is the UK police detective branch

explanation.surface: Police in a Florida town are showing little energy.
explanation.walkthrough: The Criminal Investigation Department is the plain-clothes detective branch of British police forces.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaccidity is limpness or slackness, an absence of firmness and energy.

clue.text: Crafty revolutionary paper cuts a limited order

indicators.note: cuts means slices into, so the turned paper goes inside the shortened order
limited means cut short, so the last letter of the order is dropped

parts.note: a rule is an order or regulation

indicators.note: revolutionary means turning over, so the paper's letters are reversed

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: A cunning revolutionary newspaper cuts back on a limited command.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolutionary' looks political but signals a reversal of the paper; 'limited' drops the last letter of the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Artful means cunning or sly, as in the Artful Dodger, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: Fears having to deal with old man's trousers

indicators.note: trousers is a verb here, meaning pockets, so the father's letters hold the other two

parts.note: old man is slang for father, so the old man's is dad's
re means concerning or to do with

explanation.surface: Worries about having to handle Father's trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trousers' is not clothing but a verb meaning pockets or takes in.
explanation.definitionFit: To dread something is to be afraid of it, so the verb is a synonym.

clue.text: Book when holding court

indicators.note: holding means the word for when holds the court's letters inside

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Reserving a slot while the court is in session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book' looks like a verb, to reserve; it is a book of the Bible.
explanation.definitionFit: The Acts of the Apostles is the fifth book of the New Testament.

clue.text: Not straight, like some gardens

parts.note: as means like
Kew Gardens is the Royal Botanic Gardens in west London

explanation.surface: Crooked, as some garden layouts are.
explanation.walkthrough: KEW is the famous Royal Botanic Gardens in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Askew means crooked or at an angle, out of line.

clue.text: Great stylish present for one

parts.note: in means fashionable, as in the in thing
the present is one example of a grammatical tense

explanation.surface: A wonderful fashionable gift for a single person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'present' is not a gift but the present tense.
explanation.definitionFit: Great as in great heat or great pain, meaning extreme or very strong.

clue.text: Lose oar at sea? That's rash

indicators.note: at sea means confused or all over the place, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Losing an oar out at sea would be a reckless thing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rash' looks like the adjective reckless; it is a skin rash.
explanation.definitionFit: Roseola is a viral illness of young children that produces a pink skin eruption.

clue.text: Sisters gather round for parts of speech

indicators.note: gather means collect around something, so the sisters enclose the circle

parts.note: nuns are religious sisters
a round shape is a ring, like the letter O

explanation.surface: Nuns gather round to talk about grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: Nouns are naming words, one of the grammatical categories of language.

clue.text: Outlaw some French for each disturbance

parts.note: des is French for some
per means for each, as in per person
ado is fuss or commotion

explanation.surface: Banning a few French people for each commotion they cause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outlaw' looks like a verb, to ban; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A desperado is a reckless, violent criminal, a bandit of the Wild West.
